EMBRYOLOGY__Applied / Clinical:
Why this matters: when development goes wrong you get congenital anomalies — and each one traces back to a specific step. This subtab ties embryology to the clinic: teratogens & critical periods, neural-tube defects, congenital heart disease and the classic GI, renal & facial malformations you’ll be examined on and will meet in paediatrics.
Teratogens & Critical Periods
Timing
  • Weeks 1–2 — “all-or-none” (the embryo dies or fully recovers)
  • Weeks 3–8 (embryonic/organogenesis) — the period of greatest teratogenic sensitivity (major structural defects)
  • Weeks 9+ (fetal) — growth & functional maturation (milder/functional defects)
Key teratogens
  • Alcohol → fetal alcohol syndrome (the commonest preventable cause of intellectual disability)
  • Thalidomide → limb defects (phocomelia); warfarin, ACE inhibitors, retinoids, valproate/phenytoin
  • Rubella (TORCH) → cataracts, deafness, PDA; folate deficiency → neural-tube defects
Neural Tube & CNS Defects
Failed neural tube closure (by week 4): anencephaly (cranial end) & spina bifida (caudal end).
Spina bifida — occulta (arch only), meningocele (meninges), myelomeningocele (cord + meninges → deficit).
Prevention & screening — peri-conceptional folic acid; a raised maternal AFP (open defects).
Chiari II & hydrocephalus accompany myelomeningocele.
Congenital Heart Disease
Acyanotic (L→R shunt or obstructive)
  • VSD (commonest CHD), ASD, PDA
  • The ductus arteriosus is closed by indomethacin (an NSAID) & kept open by prostaglandin E (a lifeline in duct-dependent lesions)
  • Coarctation of the aorta (obstructive, acyanotic) — radio-femoral delay, upper-limb hypertension, rib notching; critical neonatal coarctation is duct-dependent
Cyanotic (R→L shunt)
  • Tetralogy of Fallot — VSD, overriding aorta, pulmonary stenosis & RV hypertrophy (“boot-shaped” heart, “tet spells”)
  • Transposition of the great arteries — needs mixing (PDA/ASD) to survive
Gastrointestinal Anomalies
AnomalyOrigin / clue
Oesophageal atresia + TOFForegut septation defect; polyhydramnios, VACTERL
Duodenal atresiaFailed recanalisation; “double bubble”, Down syndrome
Midgut malrotation / volvulusAbnormal rotation → bilious vomiting, ischaemia
GastroschisisGut herniates right of the umbilicus, NO covering sac; usually isolated
Omphalocele (exomphalos)Gut herniates through the umbilicus, COVERED by a sac; associated anomalies/chromosomal
Meckel’s diverticulumPersistent vitelline duct (rule of 2s)
Hirschsprung’s diseaseFailed neural-crest migration → aganglionic segment
Pyloric stenosisHypertrophy → projectile non-bilious vomiting, an “olive” mass
Gastroschisis vs omphalocele. Gastroschisis = to the right of the cord, no sac, few other anomalies. Omphalocele = at the cord, covered by a sac (peritoneum/amnion), strongly associated with other & chromosomal anomalies.
Genitourinary Anomalies
Horseshoe kidney — fused lower poles caught under the inferior mesenteric artery as it ascends.
Bilateral renal agenesis — oligohydramnios → Potter sequence (pulmonary hypoplasia, limb/facial deformity).
Hypospadias — the urethral opening is on the ventral penis (failed fusion of the urethral folds).
Cryptorchidism — undescended testis; risk of infertility & malignancy.
Bladder exstrophy — a failure of the anterior abdominal/bladder wall.
Head & Neck / Face & Others
Face & neck
  • Cleft lip — failed fusion of the maxillary & medial nasal prominences
  • Cleft palate — failed fusion of the palatine shelves
  • Branchial (2nd-arch) cyst/fistula & thyroglossal cyst — persistent embryonic remnants
Other high-yield defects
  • Congenital diaphragmatic hernia (Bochdalek — posterolateral, usually left) → bowel in the thorax → pulmonary hypoplasia
  • Twinning — dizygotic (two eggs) vs monozygotic (one egg splits; chorionicity depends on timing; a late split → conjoined twins)
🧠 Mnemonics
Weeks 3–8 = organogenesis = maximum teratogen risk.
Gastroschisis — no Sac, right of cord (“Guts out, no Gift-wrap”); omphalocele = covered.
Duodenal atresia = double bubble + Down.
Prostaglandin keeps the duct Patent; indomethacin closes it.
⭐ Exam Pearls
Organogenesis (weeks 3–8) is the most teratogen-sensitive period; weeks 1–2 = all-or-none.
Fetal alcohol syndrome is the commonest preventable cause of intellectual disability.
Folic acid prevents neural-tube defects; raised maternal AFP screens for them.
VSD is the commonest CHD; Tetralogy of Fallot is the commonest cyanotic CHD.
PGE keeps the ductus open (duct-dependent lesions); indomethacin closes a PDA.
Duodenal atresia = double bubble, associated with Down syndrome.
Gastroschisis = no sac, right of the cord; omphalocele = sac-covered, more anomalies.
Hirschsprung’s = failed neural-crest migration (aganglionosis).
Renal agenesis → oligohydramnios → Potter sequence (pulmonary hypoplasia).
Bochdalek diaphragmatic hernia → bowel in the chest → pulmonary hypoplasia.
EMBRYOLOGY__General / Early Development:
The first 8 weeks in one glance: fertilisation (week 1) → a hollow blastocyst that implants and becomes a bilaminar disc (week 2) → gastrulation turns it into a trilaminar disc with three germ layers (week 3) → neurulation & folding convert a flat disc into a C-shaped embryo with organ primordia (weeks 4–8). Learn the “1-2-3” rhythm and the germ-layer derivatives — almost every exam question and anomaly hangs off this scaffold.
Week 1 — Fertilisation, Cleavage & the Blastocyst
Fertilisation → morula
  • Fertilisation occurs in the ampulla of the uterine tube; sperm penetration triggers the cortical (zona) reaction blocking polyspermy and completes meiosis II of the oocyte
  • Restores the diploid (46) number and determines genetic sex (sperm carries X or Y); the fertilised egg is the zygote
  • Cleavage — a series of mitotic divisions (no growth) producing smaller blastomeres; a solid ball of ~16 cells is the morula (~day 3–4)
Blastocyst (~day 5)
  • Fluid enters to form the blastocyst: a blastocele (cavity), an eccentric inner cell mass / embryoblast (→ embryo) and an outer trophoblast (→ placenta)
  • The blastocyst hatches from the zona pellucida (~day 5–6), which is prerequisite for implantation
  • All movement/nutrition so far is within the tube/uterus; the conceptus reaches the uterine cavity by ~day 4–5
Clinical link: if the blastocyst implants outside the uterine body — most commonly the ampulla of the tube — the result is an ectopic pregnancy (life-threatening rupture/haemorrhage). Failure to hatch/implant is a cause of early IVF failure.
Week 2 — Implantation & the Bilaminar Disc (“week of twos”)

Almost everything in week 2 comes in pairs — two trophoblast layers, two embryoblast layers, two cavities.

Trophoblast splits in two
  • Cytotrophoblast — inner, mitotically active cellular layer
  • Syncytiotrophoblast — outer multinucleate mass that invades the endometrium and secretes hCG (basis of the pregnancy test; maintains the corpus luteum)
  • Implantation is interstitial (fully embedded) by ~day 10
Embryoblast splits in two
  • Epiblast (columnar, dorsal) and hypoblast (cuboidal, ventral) = the bilaminar disc
  • Two cavities appear: the amniotic cavity (within the epiblast) and the primary yolk sac (lined by hypoblast)
  • Extra-embryonic mesoderm forms and cavitates into the chorionic cavity (extra-embryonic coelom), leaving the connecting stalk (future umbilical cord)
Week 3 — Gastrulation & the Trilaminar Disc (“week of threes”)

Gastrulation is the defining event of week 3: it converts the two-layered disc into a three-layered (trilaminar) disc and establishes the body axes.

The primitive streak
  • A midline groove — the primitive streak — appears in the epiblast, defining the craniocaudal axis, left/right and dorsal/ventral
  • Epiblast cells migrate through the streak (invagination): first replacing hypoblast to become endoderm, then forming the middle mesoderm; cells remaining in the epiblast become ectoderm
  • Thus all three germ layers derive from epiblast
Node, notochord & firsts
  • The primitive node (cranial end of the streak) forms the notochord — the midline axial rod that induces neurulation and becomes the nucleus pulposus
  • Two membranes lack mesoderm and stay bilaminar: the oropharyngeal (future mouth) and cloacal (future anus/urogenital) membranes
  • The cardiovascular system is the first organ system to function (heart beating ~day 22)
Clinical link: persistence of the primitive streak can give a sacrococcygeal teratoma (commonest tumour of the newborn). Abnormal gastrulation is associated with caudal regression / sirenomelia (maternal diabetes) and situs abnormalities.
Germ-Layer Derivatives
Germ layerSubdivisionMajor derivatives
EctodermSurface ectodermEpidermis, hair, nails, lens & cornea epithelium, inner ear, enamel, anterior pituitary, mammary/sweat/salivary glands
Neuroectoderm & neural crestNeural tube → CNS, retina, posterior pituitary. Neural crest → PNS & sensory ganglia, autonomic ganglia, adrenal medulla, melanocytes, Schwann cells, most bones of the face (membranous viscerocranium), odontoblasts, aorticopulmonary septum
MesodermParaxial (somites)Axial skeleton, skeletal muscle, dermis of back
IntermediateKidneys, gonads & genital ducts, adrenal cortex
Lateral plateCardiovascular system, blood, spleen, serous membranes (pleura/peritoneum/pericardium), limb & body-wall connective tissue
Endoderm—Epithelial lining of the GI & respiratory tracts, liver, pancreas, biliary tree, thyroid/parathyroid, thymus, bladder & urethra, tympanic cavity/auditory tube
Memory hook: “Ectoderm = attractoderm” (what attracts a partner — skin & nervous system, the outside & the brain). Endoderm = the inner tubes & their glands. Mesoderm = the meat in between (muscle, bone, blood, kidney, gonad, heart).
Neurulation & the Neural Crest (weeks 3–4)
The notochord induces overlying ectoderm to thicken into the neural plate.
The plate folds into neural folds that meet to form the neural tube (→ brain & spinal cord) — neurulation.
Neural crest cells delaminate from the fold tips and migrate widely — the “fourth germ layer”.
The cranial neuropore closes ~day 25, the caudal ~day 28; failure → anencephaly / spina bifida.
Folding & the End of the Embryonic Period (weeks 4–8)
Folding (week 4)
  • Cephalocaudal folding (head/tail) and lateral folding convert the flat trilaminar disc into a C-shaped, cylindrical embryo
  • Folding pulls the endoderm into a primitive gut tube (foregut–midgut–hindgut) and brings the connecting stalk & yolk sac together at the future umbilicus
  • The heart and oropharyngeal membrane are carried ventrally into the neck/thorax
Weeks 4–8: organogenesis
  • All major organ systems form from the germ layers — this is the embryonic period and the time of greatest teratogen sensitivity
  • Pharyngeal (branchial) arches, limb buds, face and body form; by the end of week 8 the embryo is recognisably human
  • From week 9 the fetal period begins — growth and functional maturation rather than new organ formation
Placenta & Fetal Membranes (essentials)
The placenta = fetal chorion frondosum (villous trophoblast) + maternal decidua basalis; site of gas/nutrient/waste exchange.
Chorionic villi: primary (cytotrophoblast) → secondary (+ mesoderm) → tertiary (+ fetal vessels) enable exchange.
The amnion enlarges to surround the fetus (amniotic fluid); the umbilical cord carries 2 arteries + 1 vein.
hCG from syncytiotrophoblast maintains the corpus luteum until the placenta takes over progesterone production (~week 8–10).
Mnemonics
“1-2-3” — week 1 = fertilisation/blastocyst; week 2 = bilaminar (twos); week 3 = trilaminar (threes, gastrulation).
Trophoblast layers — “Cyto is the cellular inner layer; Syncytio secretes hCG and invades.”
All three germ layers come from epiblast — the hypoblast contributes to the yolk-sac lining, not the embryo proper.
Notochord → nucleus pulposus; it induces the neural plate then largely disappears.
⭐ Exam Pearls
Fertilisation occurs in the ampulla of the uterine tube; the commonest ectopic site is also the ampulla.
Blastocyst = embryoblast (→ embryo) + trophoblast (→ placenta) + blastocele; it must hatch from the zona pellucida to implant.
Syncytiotrophoblast secretes hCG (pregnancy test) and invades the endometrium.
Gastrulation (week 3) forms the three germ layers from epiblast via the primitive streak.
The notochord induces neurulation and becomes the nucleus pulposus.
Neural crest = the “fourth germ layer”: PNS, melanocytes, adrenal medulla, aorticopulmonary septum, most facial bones.
Organogenesis (weeks 3–8) is the most teratogen-sensitive period; the fetal period begins at week 9.
The cardiovascular system is the first organ system to function (~day 22).
EMBRYOLOGY__Cardiovascular:
The heart is the first organ to function (beating ~day 22). A single heart tube loops to the right, then partitions — atrial, ventricular & outflow-tract septation — into four chambers with two great arteries. Master three things: (1) how each adult chamber/vessel derives from the primitive segments, (2) the fetal shunts (ductus venosus, foramen ovale, ductus arteriosus) and how they change at birth, and (3) how septation errors produce the congenital heart lesions you meet in paediatrics.
Heart Tube & Cardiac Looping
Origin
  • The heart arises from splanchnic (lateral plate) mesoderm — the cardiogenic area / primary heart field — cranial to the oropharyngeal membrane
  • Paired endocardial tubes fuse into a single primitive heart tube; folding brings it into the thorax
  • The tube develops five dilatations (cranial→caudal): truncus arteriosus, bulbus cordis, primitive ventricle, primitive atrium, sinus venosus
Looping (day ~23–28)
  • The tube loops to the RIGHT (D-loop) — bulbus cordis moves right/caudal, the ventricle left, and the atrium/sinus venosus move dorsocranially
  • This places the chambers in their adult topographic relationship (atria posterosuperior, ventricles anteroinferior)
  • Dextrocardia results from looping to the left (L-loop); associated with situs inversus / Kartagener syndrome
Fates of the Primitive Segments
Embryonic segmentGives rise to
Truncus arteriosusAscending aorta & pulmonary trunk (split by the aorticopulmonary/spiral septum)
Bulbus cordisProximal third → trabeculated (rough) part of the right ventricle; the smooth outflow parts: conus arteriosus (RV infundibulum) & the aortic vestibule (LV outflow)
Primitive ventricleTrabeculated (rough) part of the left ventricle
Primitive atriumTrabeculated (rough) parts of the right & left atria (the auricles/pectinate muscle)
Sinus venosus (right horn)Smooth-walled sinus venarum of the RA; the SA node; left horn → coronary sinus
Primitive pulmonary veinSmooth-walled posterior part of the left atrium
Rough vs smooth rule: the rough/trabeculated walls come from the primitive chambers; the smooth walls come from absorbed vessels (sinus venosus into RA, pulmonary veins into LA). The crista terminalis marks the RA junction.
Atrial Septation & the Foramen Ovale
The two septa
  • Septum primum grows down toward the endocardial cushions; the gap below it is the ostium primum
  • Before the ostium primum closes, the ostium secundum perforates high in the septum primum (keeps R→L flow)
  • Septum secundum grows to its right, leaving the foramen ovale; the residual septum primum acts as its one-way flap valve
Flow & closure
  • In utero oxygenated blood shunts right→left through the foramen ovale, bypassing the lungs
  • At birth left atrial pressure rises & presses septum primum against secundum → functional closure; anatomical fusion → fossa ovalis
  • Failure of fusion → a patent foramen ovale (PFO) in ~25% (usually silent; a route for paradoxical embolism)
ASD types: ostium secundum (commonest, excessive septum-primum resorption/short septum secundum) & ostium primum (failure to fuse with endocardial cushions — part of AVSD, seen in Down syndrome). ASDs are acyanotic L→R shunts presenting with a fixed split S2.
AV Canal, Ventricular & Outflow Septation
Endocardial cushions divide the AV canal into left & right orifices and form the membranous interventricular septum, the AV valves & part of the atrial septum.
The muscular IV septum grows up from the apex; the gap is closed by the membranous septum (from cushions + conotruncal ridges).
Conotruncal (bulbar) ridges spiral and fuse to form the aorticopulmonary/spiral septum, dividing the outflow into aorta & pulmonary trunk — the spiral explains why they twist around each other.
Neural crest cells populate the conotruncal ridges — errors here cause the classic conotruncal anomalies.
Septation defects: VSD (commonest CHD; usually membranous, from failed cushion/ridge closure). Failed conotruncal septation → persistent truncus arteriosus. Unequal division → Tetralogy of Fallot (antero-superior deviation) & outflow stenoses. Failed spiralling → transposition of the great arteries. Endocardial-cushion failure → AVSD (Down syndrome).
Aortic Arch Derivatives

Six pairs of pharyngeal arch arteries connect the aortic sac to the dorsal aortae; arches 1, 2 & 5 largely regress. Remember the survivors:

ArchDerivative
3rdCommon carotid & proximal internal carotid arteries
4thLeft → arch of the aorta; Right → proximal right subclavian artery
6thPulmonary arteries; on the left, also the ductus arteriosus
Recurrent laryngeal nerves follow the 6th arches: the right loses its 6th arch and hooks up under the right subclavian (4th arch), while the left stays caught under the ductus arteriosus / arch (6th) — explaining their different adult courses.
Arch anomalies: coarctation (narrowing near the ductus — radio-femoral delay, rib notching), double aortic arch (a complete vascular ring → stridor/dysphagia) & aberrant right subclavian (retro-oesophageal, not a complete ring → dysphagia lusoria), and interrupted arch.
Fetal Circulation & the Three Shunts
The three shunts
  • Ductus venosus — shunts oxygenated umbilical-vein blood past the liver into the IVC
  • Foramen ovale — shunts blood from right atrium → left atrium (bypassing the lungs)
  • Ductus arteriosus — shunts blood from the pulmonary trunk → aorta (bypassing the lungs); kept open by prostaglandin E & low O₂
The circuit
  • Most-oxygenated blood: placenta → umbilical vein → ductus venosus → IVC → RA → foramen ovale → LA → LV → aorta (to head/heart first)
  • SVC/less-oxygenated blood: RA → RV → pulmonary trunk → ductus arteriosus → descending aorta → body → 2 umbilical arteries → placenta
  • The lungs are bypassed (high pulmonary vascular resistance)
Changes at Birth & Adult Remnants
Fetal structureAdult remnant
Umbilical veinLigamentum teres hepatis (round ligament of the liver)
Ductus venosusLigamentum venosum
Ductus arteriosusLigamentum arteriosum
Foramen ovaleFossa ovalis
Umbilical arteries (distal)Medial umbilical ligaments (proximal parts stay as superior vesical arteries)
Urachus / allantoisMedian umbilical ligament
Transition: first breath → lungs expand → pulmonary vascular resistance falls & LA pressure rises → foramen ovale closes; rising O₂ & falling prostaglandins → ductus arteriosus closes (functionally in hours, anatomically in weeks). Indomethacin closes a persistent PDA; prostaglandin E keeps it open in duct-dependent lesions.
⭐ Exam Pearls
Heart = first functional organ (beats ~day 22); derived from splanchnic lateral plate mesoderm.
The heart tube loops to the RIGHT; a left (L) loop → dextrocardia.
Smooth atrial walls come from absorbed vessels (sinus venosus → RA sinus venarum; pulmonary veins → LA).
Foramen ovale = R→L shunt in utero → fossa ovalis; PFO in ~25% of adults.
Ostium secundum ASD is commonest; ostium primum ASD (AVSD) is linked to Down syndrome; fixed split S2.
Conotruncal (neural-crest) septation errors → persistent truncus, Tetralogy of Fallot, transposition.
Aortic arches: 3rd → carotids, 4th → aortic arch (L) / right subclavian, 6th → pulmonary arteries + ductus arteriosus (L).
Three shunts: ductus venosus (past liver), foramen ovale (past lungs, RA→LA), ductus arteriosus (past lungs, PT→aorta).
Remnants: umbilical vein → ligamentum teres; ductus venosus → ligamentum venosum; ductus arteriosus → ligamentum arteriosum.
EMBRYOLOGY__Respiratory:
The lower respiratory tract buds off the foregut. A respiratory diverticulum grows from the ventral foregut and is separated from the oesophagus by the tracheo-oesophageal septum — get this wrong and you have oesophageal atresia / TOF. The lung then matures through five stages (respiratory bronchioles → alveoli, surfactant from ~24 weeks) that dictate viability of a premature baby. Two golden facts: the epithelium/glands are endoderm; the cartilage, muscle & connective tissue are splanchnic mesoderm.
Origin — the Respiratory Diverticulum
Formation (~week 4)
  • A laryngotracheal groove appears in the ventral wall of the foregut, caudal to the pharynx, and evaginates as the respiratory (lung) diverticulum
  • It elongates into the laryngotracheal tube, whose distal end is the lung bud
  • The bud divides into two bronchial buds → main bronchi (the right more vertical/wider — inhaled objects lodge here)
Germ-layer origins
  • Endoderm → epithelium & glands of the larynx, trachea, bronchi & alveoli
  • Splanchnic (visceral) mesoderm → cartilage, smooth muscle, connective tissue & visceral pleura
  • The larynx cartilages/muscles come from pharyngeal arches 4 & 6 (hence recurrent & superior laryngeal innervation)
Tracheo-Oesophageal Separation
Longitudinal tracheo-oesophageal ridges fuse into the tracheo-oesophageal septum, separating the ventral trachea from the dorsal oesophagus.
Faulty septation → oesophageal atresia ± tracheo-oesophageal fistula (TOF).
Commonest type (~85%): proximal oesophageal atresia + distal TOF (fistula between distal oesophagus & trachea).
Presents with polyhydramnios, choking/frothing, an NG tube that coils, and is part of the VACTERL association.
Stages of Lung Maturation
StageTimingKey events
EmbryonicWeeks 4–7Lung bud, trachea, main/lobar/segmental bronchi (branching)
PseudoglandularWeeks 5–17Branching to terminal bronchioles; lung looks glandular; no respiration possible
CanalicularWeeks 16–26Respiratory bronchioles & primitive alveoli; vascularisation; type II pneumocytes appear (~24 wk) — end-stage viability just possible
Saccular (terminal sac)Week 24–birthTerminal sacs form; blood–air barrier thins; surfactant production rises
AlveolarWeek 32 → ~8 yearsMature alveoli multiply (most alveoli form after birth)
Memory hook: “Every Premature Child Should Ambulate” — Embryonic, Pseudoglandular, Canalicular, Saccular, Alveolar. Respiration is only possible once respiratory bronchioles + surfactant exist (late canalicular onward).
Surfactant & Neonatal Respiratory Distress
Surfactant
  • Produced by type II pneumocytes; a phospholipid (mainly dipalmitoyl-phosphatidylcholine / lecithin) that lowers alveolar surface tension and prevents collapse
  • Adequate levels usually by ~34–35 weeks; maturity gauged by a lecithin:sphingomyelin (L:S) ratio > 2
Respiratory distress syndrome (RDS)
  • Surfactant deficiency in prematurity → atelectasis, hypoxia, “ground-glass” lungs, hyaline membranes
  • Risk ↑ in prematurity, maternal diabetes (fetal hyperinsulinaemia delays surfactant), C-section
  • Prevent with antenatal maternal corticosteroids; treat with exogenous surfactant & ventilatory support
Development of the Diaphragm
Four parts: septum transversum (central tendon), pleuroperitoneal membranes, dorsal mesentery of the oesophagus (crura), and body-wall muscle.
The septum transversum starts at cervical levels (C3–5) then descends — dragging the phrenic nerve (C3,4,5) with it (“C3,4,5 keeps the diaphragm alive”).
Failure of a pleuroperitoneal membrane to close → congenital diaphragmatic hernia (usually left postero-lateral = Bochdalek).
Abdominal viscera in the chest → pulmonary hypoplasia (the lung can't expand) — the main cause of death.
Congenital Respiratory Anomalies
AnomalyKey features
Oesophageal atresia / TOFFaulty TE septum; polyhydramnios, coiled NG tube, aspiration; VACTERL
Congenital diaphragmatic hernia (Bochdalek)Failed pleuroperitoneal membrane; bowel in chest → pulmonary hypoplasia & respiratory distress
Respiratory distress syndromeSurfactant deficiency of prematurity; ground-glass lungs
Pulmonary hypoplasiaUnderdeveloped lungs — from CDH, oligohydramnios (Potter sequence) or space-occupying lesions
Congenital pulmonary airway malformation (CPAM/CCAM)Cystic mass of dysplastic terminal airways; may cause distress or infection
Bronchogenic cyst / pulmonary sequestrationAbnormal foregut budding; sequestration has a systemic (aortic) blood supply & no bronchial connection
⭐ Exam Pearls
The lower respiratory tract buds from the ventral foregut (endoderm = epithelium/glands; splanchnic mesoderm = cartilage/muscle/pleura).
Faulty tracheo-oesophageal septum → oesophageal atresia + distal TOF (commonest); polyhydramnios, coiled NG tube, VACTERL.
Five stages: Embryonic, Pseudoglandular, Canalicular, Saccular, Alveolar (“Every Premature Child Should Ambulate”).
Respiration first possible in the late canalicular stage (respiratory bronchioles + early surfactant, ~24 wk).
Surfactant = type II pneumocytes (lecithin); adequate ~34–35 wk; L:S ratio >2 = maturity.
Maternal diabetes and prematurity increase RDS risk; antenatal steroids accelerate surfactant.
Most alveoli form after birth (alveolar stage to ~8 years).
Diaphragm = septum transversum + pleuroperitoneal membranes + oesophageal mesentery + body wall; phrenic nerve C3,4,5.
Bochdalek (left postero-lateral) CDH → pulmonary hypoplasia.
EMBRYOLOGY__Gastrointestinal:
The gut is a single endodermal tube divided into foregut, midgut & hindgut — each with its own artery, nerve supply & pain referral. Two dynamic events dominate: the stomach rotates (building the lesser sac & explaining vagal “left→anterior”), and the midgut herniates, rotates 270° & returns. Get the three arteries, the rotations, and the cloacal partition and the classic anomalies (malrotation, atresias, omphalocele vs gastroschisis, Meckel’s, Hirschsprung, imperforate anus) fall into place.
Gut Divisions, Arteries & Boundaries
DivisionArteryExtentReferred pain
ForegutCoeliac trunk (T12)Oesophagus → proximal duodenum (to the major duodenal papilla); + liver, gallbladder, pancreas, spleenEpigastric
MidgutSMA (L1)Distal duodenum → proximal ⅔ of transverse colonPeriumbilical
HindgutIMA (L3)Distal ⅓ transverse colon → upper anal canal (to the pectinate line)Suprapubic / hypogastric
The boundary rule: the artery changes where the gut region changes. The foregut–midgut junction is at the major duodenal papilla (2nd part of duodenum); the midgut–hindgut junction is at the proximal ⅔ / distal ⅓ of the transverse colon. The spleen is mesodermal (dorsal mesogastrium) but takes a foregut (coeliac) supply.
Foregut — Stomach Rotation & the Lesser Sac
Two rotations
  • 90° clockwise about a longitudinal axis: the left side becomes anterior — so the left vagus supplies the anterior wall & the right vagus the posterior; the greater curvature (originally the dorsal border) swings to the left and the lesser curvature to the right
  • The faster-growing dorsal border becomes the greater curvature; the ventral border the lesser curvature
  • A slight anteroposterior tilt carries the pylorus up/right and the cardia down/left
Mesenteries & sac
  • Rotation pulls the dorsal mesogastrium left, creating the lesser sac (omental bursa) behind the stomach
  • The dorsal mesogastrium forms the greater omentum & gastrosplenic/splenorenal ligaments; the spleen develops within it
  • The ventral mesogastrium forms the lesser omentum & falciform ligament; the liver grows into it
Foregut — Liver, Pancreas & Spleen
The hepatic diverticulum buds from the ventral foregut into the septum transversum → liver, gallbladder & biliary tree; haematopoiesis begins here.
The pancreas forms from a ventral & a dorsal bud. The ventral bud rotates posteriorly to fuse with the dorsal bud → uncinate process & inferior head.
The main pancreatic duct = distal dorsal duct + ventral duct; the proximal dorsal duct persists as the accessory duct.
Failure of the ventral bud to rotate normally → annular pancreas (a ring around the duodenum → obstruction).
Pancreas divisum (commonest pancreatic variant) — the ducts fail to fuse, so most drainage is via the small accessory papilla.
Midgut — Herniation & Rotation
The sequence
  • Week 6: rapid growth (+ the large liver) forces physiological herniation of the midgut into the umbilical cord around the SMA axis
  • While herniated it rotates 90° anticlockwise (viewed from the front)
  • Week 10: the gut returns to the abdomen, rotating a further 180° anticlockwise — a total of 270° anticlockwise
  • The jejunum returns first (to the left); the caecum returns last and descends to the right iliac fossa
Consequences
  • Rotation places the transverse colon anterior to the duodenum & SMA
  • The vitelline (omphalomesenteric) duct normally regresses; a remnant = Meckel’s diverticulum
  • Failure/incomplete rotation → malrotation (with Ladd’s bands & risk of midgut volvulus)
Hindgut & Partition of the Cloaca
The hindgut ends in the cloaca, which the urorectal septum divides into a ventral urogenital sinus and a dorsal anorectal canal.
The septum meets the cloacal membrane at the perineal body; the membrane breaks down to open the anus & urogenital tract.
The pectinate (dentate) line marks the old cloacal membrane — the endoderm/ectoderm junction (hindgut vs proctodeum), explaining the split blood/nerve/lymph supply of the anal canal.
Failure of urorectal septum/cloacal development → anorectal malformations (imperforate anus, rectovesical/rectovaginal fistulae).
Congenital GI Anomalies
AnomalyMechanism & features
Hypertrophic pyloric stenosisPyloric muscle hypertrophy (not a true embryological defect) — projectile non-bilious vomiting at 3–6 weeks, palpable “olive”, commoner in first-born males
Duodenal atresiaFailed recanalisation of the duodenum — bilious vomiting, “double-bubble”, associated with Down syndrome & polyhydramnios
Jejunoileal atresiaUsually a vascular accident (“apple-peel” atresia) — distal bilious obstruction
Malrotation ± volvulusIncomplete 270° rotation; Ladd’s bands; midgut volvulus is a surgical emergency (ischaemia)
Omphalocele (exomphalos)Failure of gut to return — herniation into the cord, covered by peritoneum/amnion, midline; strong chromosomal/associated anomalies
GastroschisisRight para-umbilical body-wall defect, no covering sac; usually isolated
Meckel’s diverticulumPersistent vitelline duct — “rule of 2s”; may contain ectopic gastric/pancreatic tissue → painless PR bleeding
Hirschsprung diseaseFailed neural-crest migration → aganglionic distal colon → failure to pass meconium, constipation; rectal biopsy
Imperforate anus / anorectal malformationAbnormal urorectal septum / cloacal development ± fistula; part of VACTERL
Biliary atresiaObliteration of extrahepatic bile ducts → persistent neonatal jaundice, pale stools; needs early Kasai
⭐ Exam Pearls
Foregut = coeliac (epigastric pain); midgut = SMA (periumbilical); hindgut = IMA (suprapubic).
Foregut ends at the major duodenal papilla; midgut ends at the proximal ⅔ transverse colon; hindgut ends at the pectinate line.
Stomach rotates 90° clockwise → left vagus supplies the anterior wall; the lesser sac forms behind it.
Ventral mesogastrium → lesser omentum + falciform ligament (liver); dorsal mesogastrium → greater omentum + spleen.
Ventral + dorsal pancreatic buds fuse; failure of ventral-bud rotation → annular pancreas; non-fusion → pancreas divisum.
Midgut herniates (~wk 6), rotates 270° anticlockwise around the SMA, returns (~wk 10); jejunum first, caecum last to RIF.
Duodenal atresia = double-bubble + Down; jejunoileal atresia = apple-peel (vascular).
Omphalocele = sac-covered + anomalies; gastroschisis = no sac, right of cord, isolated.
Persistent vitelline duct → Meckel's; failed neural-crest migration → Hirschsprung's; abnormal urorectal septum → imperforate anus.
EMBRYOLOGY__Genitourinary:
The urinary & genital systems share an origin — intermediate mesoderm. The kidney is built and rebuilt three times (pro-, meso-, metanephros); the ureteric bud meets the metanephric blastema to make the definitive kidney, which ascends and re-plumbs its blood supply. Genital development runs from an indifferent stage — SRY flips the switch: testis → testosterone + AMH + DHT (Wolffian kept, Müllerian lost); no SRY → ovary & the default female pathway (Müllerian kept). Nail the duct fates and the anomalies (horseshoe kidney, Potter, hypospadias, cryptorchidism, CAH, AIS, uterine fusion defects) follow.
Three Kidney Systems
SystemFate
PronephrosRudimentary & non-functional; degenerates (week 4)
MesonephrosTemporarily functional; largely regresses. Its mesonephric (Wolffian) duct persists (→ male genital ducts & ureteric bud origin)
MetanephrosThe definitive kidney (functions from ~week 10); forms from the ureteric bud + metanephric blastema
All arise from intermediate mesoderm; development proceeds cranial → caudal, each system inducing the next.
The Definitive Kidney — Two Origins
Ureteric bud → collecting system
  • An outgrowth of the mesonephric duct that induces the blastema
  • Forms the ureter, renal pelvis, major & minor calyces & collecting ducts
  • Repeated branching drives nephron formation — too little branching = renal hypoplasia
Metanephric blastema → nephron
  • A cap of metanephric mesoderm induced by the bud
  • Forms the nephron: glomerulus, PCT, loop of Henle & DCT (up to the connecting tubule)
  • Reciprocal induction — each tissue signals the other; failure → renal agenesis
Where they meet: the collecting duct (bud) joins the DCT (blastema) — the classic exam split. The kidney starts functioning ~week 10, producing urine into the amniotic fluid.
Ascent & Changing Blood Supply
The metanephros forms in the pelvis and ascends to the lumbar region (relative caudal growth of the embryo).
As it ascends it takes blood from progressively higher vessels; lower ones normally regress, leaving the final renal artery at ~L2.
Persistent lower vessels → accessory (polar) renal arteries (common; may cross & obstruct the PUJ).
The hilum rotates 90° medially during ascent, so the hilum faces medially.
Bladder, Urethra & the Urogenital Sinus
Urogenital sinus divisions
  • The urorectal septum splits the cloaca; its ventral part is the urogenital sinus
  • Vesical part → bladder (continuous with the allantois at the apex → urachus / median umbilical ligament)
  • Pelvic part → prostatic & membranous urethra (male); entire female urethra
  • Phallic part → spongy (penile) urethra / vaginal vestibule
The trigone & epithelium
  • Most bladder epithelium is endoderm; the trigone is derived from absorbed mesonephric ducts (mesoderm)
  • Absorption of the ducts brings the ureters to open separately & superolaterally, while the ducts open lower (→ ejaculatory ducts in the male)
Gonad & Genital Duct Differentiation
Male (SRY present)
  • SRY on the Y → testis-determining factor → medullary (testis) cords → Sertoli cells; Leydig cells arise from the surrounding gonadal-ridge mesenchyme
  • Sertoli cells → AMH (anti-Müllerian hormone) → Müllerian (paramesonephric) ducts regress
  • Leydig cells → testosterone → Wolffian (mesonephric) ducts persist → epididymis, vas deferens, seminal vesicle, ejaculatory duct
  • DHT (5α-reductase) → prostate, penis & scrotum
Female (no SRY)
  • No SRY → cortical cords → ovary; germ cells needed to maintain it (else streak gonad)
  • No AMH → Müllerian ducts persist → uterine tubes, uterus, cervix & upper vagina (fused caudally)
  • No testosterone → Wolffian ducts regress (remnants: Gartner’s duct cyst)
  • The lower vagina forms from the sinovaginal bulbs (urogenital sinus)
Golden rule: the female pattern is the default; masculinisation needs testis products. AMH removes Müllerian; testosterone keeps Wolffian; DHT builds the external male genitalia & prostate.
External Genitalia & Gonadal Descent
Indifferent parts: genital tubercle, urogenital folds, labioscrotal swellings.
Male (DHT): tubercle → glans/penis; urogenital folds fuse → penile urethra; labioscrotal swellings fuse → scrotum.
Female: tubercle → clitoris; folds → labia minora (unfused); swellings → labia majora.
Descent: the gubernaculum guides the testis through the inguinal canal into the scrotum (by birth); in the female it becomes the ovarian ligament + round ligament of the uterus.
Congenital GU Anomalies
AnomalyMechanism & features
Horseshoe kidneyLower poles fuse; ascent arrested by the inferior mesenteric artery → low-lying kidney
Renal agenesis (bilateral)Ureteric bud fails to induce blastema → no kidney → oligohydramnios → Potter sequence (pulmonary hypoplasia)
Duplex / ectopic ureterPremature/split ureteric bud → duplicated system; ectopic opening → incontinence
Pelvi-ureteric junction (PUJ) obstructionCommonest cause of antenatal hydronephrosis; ± crossing accessory vessel
Polycystic kidney diseaseAutosomal recessive (infantile) — bilateral enlarged cystic kidneys
Bladder exstrophyFailure of anterior abdominal/bladder wall (cloacal membrane defect) → exposed bladder mucosa
Urachal fistula / cystPersistent urachus → urine leak from umbilicus (fistula) or a midline cyst
HypospadiasFailed fusion of the urethral folds → ventral urethral opening (do not circumcise)
EpispadiasUrethra opens on the dorsum of the penis (associated with exstrophy)
CryptorchidismUndescended testis → infertility & ↑ malignancy risk; orchidopexy
Congenital adrenal hyperplasia (21-hydroxylase)Excess androgens → virilisation of a female fetus (ambiguous genitalia); salt-wasting
Androgen insensitivity (AIS)46,XY, defective androgen receptor → female phenotype, testes present, no uterus (AMH still acts)
Uterine (Müllerian) anomaliesFusion defects → bicornuate / didelphys uterus; failure of septal resorption → septate uterus
⭐ Exam Pearls
All GU structures arise from intermediate mesoderm; kidneys form pro-→meso-→metanephros (cranial to caudal).
Ureteric bud → collecting system (ureter→collecting ducts); metanephric blastema → nephron (glomerulus→DCT); they meet at the collecting duct/DCT.
The kidney ascends from pelvis to L2 and its blood supply re-plumbs; persistent vessels → accessory renal arteries.
Horseshoe kidney is trapped under the IMA; bilateral renal agenesis → Potter sequence.
Bladder trigone = mesoderm (mesonephric ducts); rest of bladder epithelium = endoderm; apex → urachus.
SRY → testis; Sertoli AMH removes Müllerian ducts; Leydig testosterone keeps Wolffian; DHT builds external male genitalia/prostate.
Female is the default pathway (Müllerian kept, Wolffian regresses); Wolffian remnant = Gartner's duct cyst.
Hypospadias = failed urethral fold fusion (ventral); epispadias = dorsal (with exstrophy).
CAH virilises a female fetus; AIS (46,XY) = female phenotype with testes and no uterus.
EMBRYOLOGY__Head & Neck:
The head & neck is built from the pharyngeal apparatus. Six arches (mesoderm + neural crest) each carry a cartilage, muscle, nerve & artery; between them are endodermal pouches and ectodermal clefts. Learn the arch table (nerve + muscle + cartilage), the pouch derivatives (ear, tonsil, parathyroids, thymus), and the tongue/thyroid/face stories — and the anomalies (cleft lip/palate, branchial cyst, DiGeorge, thyroglossal cyst) follow directly.
Pharyngeal Arches — the Master Table

There are six arches but the 5th regresses (no derivatives). Each arch’s muscles carry their arch nerve wherever they migrate.

ArchNerveMusclesSkeletal / cartilage
1st (mandibular)CN V₃ (+ V₂)Muscles of mastication, mylohyoid, ant. belly digastric, tensor tympani, tensor veli palatiniMeckel’s cartilage → malleus, incus & sphenomandibular ligament; first-arch mesenchyme → mandible, maxilla & zygoma (membranous ossification)
2nd (hyoid)CN VIIMuscles of facial expression, stapedius, stylohyoid, post. belly digastricReichert’s cartilage → stapes, styloid process, stylohyoid ligament, lesser horn & upper hyoid
3rdCN IXStylopharyngeusGreater horn & lower body of hyoid
4thCN X — superior laryngealPharyngeal constrictors, cricothyroid, levator veli palatiniThyroid cartilage
6thCN X — recurrent laryngealIntrinsic muscles of the larynx (except cricothyroid)Cricoid, arytenoid, corniculate & cuneiform cartilages
Nerve mnemonic: arches 1-2-3-4/6 → V₃, VII, IX, X. Cricothyroid (4th, superior laryngeal) is the odd one out among laryngeal muscles — all the rest are 6th arch (recurrent laryngeal).
Pharyngeal Pouches (endoderm)
PouchDerivatives
1stMiddle ear cavity, mastoid antrum & auditory (Eustachian) tube (tubotympanic recess)
2ndPalatine tonsil (crypts & epithelium)
3rdInferior parathyroids (dorsal) & the thymus (ventral)
4thSuperior parathyroids (dorsal) & the ultimopharyngeal body → parafollicular C cells of the thyroid
Migration twist: the 3rd-pouch structures migrate furthest — the thymus & inferior parathyroids are dragged caudally past the 4th-pouch derivatives, so the inferior parathyroids end up below the superior ones (3rd starts above but finishes below).
Pharyngeal Clefts (ectoderm) & Membranes
Only the 1st cleft persists → the external acoustic meatus.
Clefts 2–4 are buried by the overgrowing 2nd arch, forming the transient cervical sinus, which normally obliterates.
The 1st pharyngeal membrane (ecto + endoderm, with mesoderm) → the tympanic membrane.
A persistent cervical sinus → branchial cyst/fistula/sinus (lateral neck, anterior to sternocleidomastoid).
Development of the Tongue
Mucosa (arches → nerves)
  • Anterior ⅔: two lateral lingual swellings + tuberculum impar (arch 1) → general sensation V₃ (lingual), taste chorda tympani (VII)
  • Posterior ⅓: hypobranchial eminence (arch 3, some 4; the 2nd-arch copula is overgrown) → general & taste IX (with a small area to X)
  • The two parts meet at the terminal sulcus (apex = foramen caecum)
Muscles
  • Nearly all tongue muscle comes from occipital myotomes (somites) that migrate forward
  • Hence motor supply is CN XII (hypoglossal) — except palatoglossus (CN X)
Thyroid Gland
The thyroid begins as a midline endodermal diverticulum at the foramen caecum (junction of anterior ⅔ / posterior ⅓ of the tongue).
It descends in front of the pharynx via the thyroglossal duct, which normally disappears; the pyramidal lobe is a remnant.
A persistent duct → thyroglossal cyst (midline, moves up on swallowing & tongue protrusion).
Arrested descent → lingual/ectopic thyroid (may be the only functioning thyroid tissue — beware before excising).
Face & Palate
Facial prominences
  • Frontonasal prominence → forehead, bridge of nose, medial & lateral nasal prominences
  • Medial nasal prominences fuse → intermaxillary segment → philtrum, 4 incisors & primary palate
  • Maxillary prominences → cheeks, lateral upper lip; mandibular prominences → lower jaw/lip
  • Lateral nasal prominences → alae of the nose (separated from maxillary by the nasolacrimal groove)
Palate
  • Primary palate — from the intermaxillary segment (anterior, pre-incisive)
  • Secondary palate — the two palatine shelves of the maxillary prominences elevate & fuse (with each other & the nasal septum)
  • Fusion runs front → back; the incisive foramen is the landmark dividing the primary (anterior) from the secondary palate
Clefts: cleft lip = failure of fusion of the maxillary + medial nasal prominence (± primary palate). Cleft palate = failure of fusion of the palatine shelves (secondary palate). They occur separately or together; cleft lip is commoner in males, isolated cleft palate in females.
Congenital Head & Neck Anomalies
AnomalyMechanism & features
Cleft lip / palateFailed prominence/shelf fusion (see above); commonest craniofacial anomaly
Branchial (cervical) cystPersistent cervical sinus (2nd cleft) → painless fluctuant lump anterior to sternocleidomastoid; a fistula opens onto the skin
DiGeorge syndrome (22q11 del)Failure of 3rd & 4th pouches → thymic & parathyroid aplasia → T-cell immunodeficiency & hypocalcaemia (+ cardiac conotruncal defects)
Thyroglossal duct cystPersistent thyroglossal duct → midline cyst that elevates on tongue protrusion
Ectopic / lingual thyroidArrested descent; may be the only functioning thyroid tissue
Treacher Collins syndrome1st-arch (neural crest) defect → malar/mandibular hypoplasia, ear anomalies
Pierre Robin sequenceMicrognathia → glossoptosis → airway obstruction & cleft palate
⭐ Exam Pearls
Arch nerves 1→2→3→4→6 = V₃, VII, IX, X(superior laryngeal), X(recurrent laryngeal); the 5th arch has no derivatives.
Arch 1 → malleus & incus + muscles of mastication (V₃); arch 2 → stapes + muscles of facial expression (VII).
Cricothyroid is the only laryngeal muscle from the 4th arch (superior laryngeal); all others are 6th arch (recurrent laryngeal).
Pouches: 1 → middle ear/auditory tube; 2 → palatine tonsil; 3 → inferior parathyroids + thymus; 4 → superior parathyroids + C cells.
Inferior parathyroids (3rd pouch) descend past the superior (4th pouch) — a common ectopic-gland pitfall.
1st cleft → external acoustic meatus; other clefts form the cervical sinus (→ branchial cyst if persistent).
Tongue: anterior ⅔ sensation V₃/taste chorda tympani (VII); posterior ⅓ IX; muscles CN XII (except palatoglossus, X).
Thyroid descends from the foramen caecum via the thyroglossal duct → thyroglossal cyst / lingual thyroid.
DiGeorge = 3rd/4th pouch failure → no thymus/parathyroids (immunodeficiency + hypocalcaemia); 22q11 deletion.
EMBRYOLOGY__Nervous System:
The whole CNS is a modified tube. Neurulation makes a neural tube (→ CNS) & neural crest (→ PNS). The tube’s wall organises into a dorsal alar plate (sensory) and ventral basal plate (motor) split by the sulcus limitans; its cranial end balloons into 3 → 5 brain vesicles whose cavities become the ventricles. Master the vesicle-derivative-ventricle map, the alar/basal rule, the neural-crest & pituitary origins, and the neural-tube defects.
From Neural Plate to Neural Tube
Neurulation
  • The notochord induces the overlying ectoderm to form the neural plate (neuroectoderm)
  • The plate folds into neural folds that fuse into the neural tube (→ brain & spinal cord)
  • The cranial neuropore closes ~day 25, the caudal ~day 28
Neural crest
  • Cells at the fold tips break away as the neural crest and migrate widely
  • They form most of the peripheral nervous system & more (see below)
  • The tube’s lumen becomes the ventricular system & central canal, lined by ependyma
Wall of the Neural Tube — Alar & Basal Plates
Alar plate (dorsal) → sensory neurons; basal plate (ventral) → motor neurons.
The sulcus limitans is the groove separating them (in the cord & brainstem).
Roof & floor plates are non-neuronal; the floor plate helps organise crossing axons.
Three layers form the wall: ventricular (ependymal), mantle (grey matter) & marginal (white matter) zones.
Histogenesis: the neuroepithelium makes neurons and macroglia (astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, ependyma). Microglia are the exception — they come from mesoderm (blood monocytes), not neuroectoderm.
Brain Vesicles & Their Derivatives
Primary (3)Secondary (5)DerivativesCavity → ventricle
Prosencephalon
(forebrain)		TelencephalonCerebral hemispheres, cortex & basal gangliaLateral ventricles
DiencephalonThalamus, hypothalamus, retina & optic nerve, pineal, posterior pituitaryThird ventricle
Mesencephalon
(midbrain)		MesencephalonMidbrain (tectum, tegmentum, cerebral peduncles)Cerebral aqueduct
Rhombencephalon
(hindbrain)		MetencephalonPons & cerebellumFourth ventricle
MyelencephalonMedulla oblongata
Flexures: the tube bends at the cephalic & cervical flexures (concave ventrally) and the pontine flexure (concave dorsally), which opens the roof of the 4th ventricle.
The Pituitary — a Dual Origin
Anterior lobe (adenohypophysis)
  • From Rathke’s pouch — an upgrowth of oral (surface) ectoderm (roof of the stomodeum)
  • Forms the pars distalis, pars intermedia & pars tuberalis
  • A remnant → a craniopharyngioma (calcified suprasellar tumour)
Posterior lobe (neurohypophysis)
  • A downgrowth of neuroectoderm from the diencephalon (infundibulum)
  • Forms the pars nervosa & infundibular stalk
  • Stores/releases ADH & oxytocin made in the hypothalamus
Spinal Cord — Plates & Ascent
In the cord the alar plates → dorsal (sensory) horns, the basal plates → ventral (motor) horns; between them (T1–L2) the small lateral horn = sympathetic outflow.
“Ascent of the cord”: the vertebral column grows faster than the cord, so the conus medullaris rises from ~L3 at birth to L1/L2 in the adult.
This differential growth stretches the roots into the cauda equina and leaves the filum terminale.
A lumbar puncture is done below L2 (L3/4 or L4/5) to avoid the cord — a direct consequence of the ascent.
Neural Crest — the “Fourth Germ Layer”
PNS: dorsal root & cranial sensory ganglia, autonomic (sympathetic & parasympathetic) ganglia, all Schwann cells.
Endocrine: adrenal medulla (chromaffin cells) & thyroid parafollicular C cells.
Pigment/skin: melanocytes.
Head: most facial bones & connective tissue, odontoblasts, much of the cranial leptomeninges (pia/arachnoid), & the aorticopulmonary septum.
Neurocristopathies: failure of neural-crest migration/derivatives underlies Hirschsprung disease (aganglionosis), DiGeorge syndrome, neurofibromatosis & phaeochromocytoma/neuroblastoma.
Neural Tube Defects & CNS Malformations
DefectMechanism & features
AnencephalyFailure of the cranial (rostral) neuropore to close → absent forebrain/calvaria; incompatible with life; polyhydramnios, raised AFP
Spina bifida occultaFailure of vertebral arch fusion only (skin-covered; hair tuft/dimple) — cord & meninges intact
MeningoceleMeninges herniate through the defect (cord in place)
MyelomeningoceleMeninges and neural tissue herniate → neurological deficit; the commonest severe open form
Chiari II (Arnold–Chiari)Herniation of the cerebellar vermis/brainstem through the foramen magnum → hydrocephalus; accompanies myelomeningocele
HoloprosencephalyFailure of the forebrain to cleave into two hemispheres → midline facial defects (± single ventricle); linked to trisomy 13 & alcohol
Dandy–Walker malformationAgenesis of the cerebellar vermis with a large posterior fossa cyst (4th ventricle) → hydrocephalus
HydrocephalusCSF accumulation (e.g. aqueductal stenosis) → enlarging head/ventricles
Prevention & screening: peri-conceptional folic acid reduces NTDs; open defects raise maternal serum & amniotic AFP (and acetylcholinesterase) and are seen on ultrasound; closed defects do not raise AFP.
⭐ Exam Pearls
Neural tube → CNS; neural crest → PNS. Alar plate = sensory (dorsal); basal plate = motor (ventral); sulcus limitans divides them.
Microglia are the odd glia out — derived from mesoderm (monocytes), not neuroectoderm.
Telencephalon → hemispheres/basal ganglia (lateral ventricles); diencephalon → thalamus/hypothalamus/retina/posterior pituitary (3rd ventricle).
Metencephalon → pons + cerebellum; myelencephalon → medulla (both share the 4th ventricle); mesencephalon → cerebral aqueduct.
Anterior pituitary from Rathke's pouch (oral ectoderm); posterior pituitary from the diencephalon (neuroectoderm); Rathke remnant → craniopharyngioma.
The cord “ascends” from ~L3 at birth to L1/L2 in the adult → LP done below L2.
Anencephaly = cranial neuropore failure; spina bifida cystica = caudal neuropore failure (occulta = vertebral arch failure); folic acid reduces both.
Open NTDs raise AFP; myelomeningocele accompanies Chiari II + hydrocephalus.
Holoprosencephaly (trisomy 13/alcohol) = failure of forebrain cleavage with midline facial defects.
EMBRYOLOGY__Musculoskeletal & Limbs:
Bones, muscle & dermis are built from mesoderm — mostly the somites. Paraxial mesoderm segments into somites that split into sclerotome (bone), myotome (muscle) & dermatome (dermis). Limbs bud from lateral plate mesoderm (skeleton) invaded by somite-derived muscle, patterned by three signalling centres — AER (length), ZPA/Shh (thumb→little finger) & Wnt (back vs palm). Learn somite derivatives, membranous vs endochondral ossification, the limb signalling centres & rotation, and the anomalies (clubfoot, DDH, polydactyly, achondroplasia).
Somites & Their Derivatives
Formation
  • Paraxial mesoderm segments craniocaudally into pairs of somites (~day 20 onward; used to “age” an embryo)
  • Each somite differentiates into three parts
  • The most cranial paraxial mesoderm stays unsegmented as somitomeres (head muscles)
Three derivatives
  • Sclerotome → vertebrae & ribs (axial skeleton)
  • Myotome → skeletal muscle (epaxial → back extensors; hypaxial → body wall & limb muscle)
  • Dermatome → dermis of the back (dorsal skin)
Mnemonic: a somite gives “S-M-D” — Sclerotome (skeleton), Myotome (muscle), Dermatome (dermis).
Vertebrae & Resegmentation
Each vertebra forms by resegmentation: the caudal half of one sclerotome fuses with the cranial half of the next.
This shift lets segmental (spinal) nerves exit between vertebrae and intersegmental arteries cross the vertebral bodies.
The notochord persists only as the nucleus pulposus of the intervertebral disc (the annulus fibrosus is sclerotome).
A defect → hemivertebra (→ congenital scoliosis) or fusion anomalies (e.g. Klippel–Feil).
The Skull
PartOrigin & ossification
Neurocranium — flat bones (calvaria)Paraxial mesoderm + neural crest; intramembranous ossification (with fontanelles & sutures)
Neurocranium — base (chondrocranium)Paraxial mesoderm + neural crest; endochondral ossification
Viscerocranium (facial skeleton)Neural crest via the pharyngeal arches (mostly intramembranous)
Clinical: the soft fontanelles allow moulding & brain growth (anterior closes ~18 months). Premature suture fusion → craniosynostosis (abnormal skull shape).
Bone Formation — Two Routes
Intramembranous
  • Bone laid down directly in mesenchyme (no cartilage model)
  • Forms the flat bones of the skull, the facial bones & the clavicle (mostly — the clavicular ends ossify endochondrally)
Endochondral
  • Bone replaces a hyaline cartilage model
  • Forms long bones, vertebrae, ribs & the skull base
  • Primary centre (diaphysis) & later secondary centres (epiphyses); growth at the epiphyseal (growth) plate
Clinical: achondroplasia (activating FGFR3 mutation) impairs endochondral growth → short (rhizomelic) limbs with a relatively normal trunk but a large head (frontal bossing & midface hypoplasia). Osteogenesis imperfecta (type I collagen) → brittle bones & blue sclerae.
Limb Development & Signalling Centres

Limb buds appear in week 4 (upper before lower) from lateral plate mesoderm (bones & connective tissue) covered by ectoderm; myoblasts migrate in from the somites.

CentreSignalAxis controlled
Apical ectodermal ridge (AER)FGFsProximodistal (outgrowth/length: stylopod → zeugopod → autopod)
Zone of polarising activity (ZPA)Sonic hedgehog (Shh)Anteroposterior (thumb → little finger)
Dorsal ectodermWnt7aDorsoventral (back of hand vs palm)
Digit separation: the webs between digits are removed by apoptosis (programmed cell death); failure → syndactyly. Extra ZPA signalling → polydactyly.
Limb Rotation
Limbs begin with flexor surfaces facing ventrally; they then rotate in opposite directions.
The upper limb rotates laterally → the elbow points backward & the extensor (dorsal) surface faces posteriorly; thumb lies laterally.
The lower limb rotates medially → the knee points forward & the great toe lies medially.
Rotation explains the spiral pattern of the limb dermatomes and the opposite positions of the elbow and knee.
Origins of Muscle
Skeletal muscle — from myotomes/somites (trunk & limbs) and pharyngeal arches (head & neck); extraocular from somitomeres/prechordal, tongue from occipital somites.
Smooth muscle — mostly from splanchnic mesoderm (gut/vessel wall); the iris sphincter & dilator pupillae are the exception (neuroectoderm of the optic cup).
Cardiac muscle — from splanchnic mesoderm surrounding the heart tube.
Each migrating muscle carries its nerve — the reason the diaphragm (C3,4,5) and other muscles keep a “distant” supply.
Congenital MSK & Limb Anomalies
AnomalyMechanism & features
Amelia / meromeliaAbsent (amelia) or partial (meromelia) limb
PhocomeliaAbsent long bones (“flipper” limbs) — classically thalidomide (limb-bud window, weeks 4–6)
SyndactylyFailure of interdigital apoptosis → fused digits
PolydactylyExtra digits (extra ZPA/Shh signalling)
Talipes equinovarus (clubfoot)Inverted, plantarflexed, adducted foot; commoner in males
Developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH)Shallow acetabulum/dislocatable hip; screen with Ortolani/Barlow & USS (breech, female, first-born)
Amniotic band syndromeFibrous amniotic bands constrict limbs/digits → amputations/rings
AchondroplasiaFGFR3 mutation → defective endochondral ossification → short limbs (autosomal dominant)
Cleidocranial dysplasiaDefective intramembranous/skull & absent/hypoplastic clavicles (RUNX2)
Sirenomelia (mermaid syndrome)Fusion of the lower limbs — caudal mesoderm defect (linked to maternal diabetes)
⭐ Exam Pearls
Somite = sclerotome (vertebrae/ribs) + myotome (skeletal muscle) + dermatome (dorsal dermis).
Vertebrae form by resegmentation (caudal half of one + cranial half of next) so nerves exit between them; notochord → nucleus pulposus.
Intramembranous ossification = flat skull bones, face & clavicle; endochondral = long bones, vertebrae, ribs & skull base.
Limb skeleton from lateral plate mesoderm; limb muscle from somites (myoblasts migrate in).
AER (FGF) → proximodistal; ZPA (Shh) → anteroposterior (thumb→little finger); Wnt7a → dorsoventral.
Interdigital apoptosis separates the digits; failure → syndactyly; extra ZPA → polydactyly.
Upper limb rotates laterally (elbow back); lower limb rotates medially (knee forward) — explains dermatome spiralling.
Achondroplasia = FGFR3, endochondral defect, short limbs/normal trunk; thalidomide → phocomelia.
Cleidocranial dysplasia → absent clavicles; osteogenesis imperfecta → brittle bones + blue sclerae.
